cues.text: A Gathering With One Purpose
From the very first years of the Church, believers have gathered to settle hard questions together rather than alone.
The Apostles did exactly this in Jerusalem around the year 49, meeting to decide whether Gentile converts had to keep the Mosaic Law (Acts 15).
Every council since has followed that same basic pattern: bishops, gathered in one place, seeking the mind of the Church on a question the whole Church needs answered.
A council is not a debate settled by majority vote, the way a parliament might settle a law.
It is an exercise of the teaching office Christ gave His Church — bishops in union with one another and, for the councils that bind the whole Church, in union with the Pope.
Ecumenical and Regional — Not the Same Thing
This timeline sorts every council into one of two kinds, and the difference matters more than it might first appear.
An ecumenical council gathers bishops from the whole Church and, once its decrees are confirmed by the Pope, binds Catholics everywhere.
A regional or particular council — a synod of one province, one kingdom, one local church — settles matters for that place alone.
The Catholic Church recognizes twenty-one ecumenical councils, from Nicaea in 325 to the Second Vatican Council in 1962 to 1965.

Hundreds of regional councils and synods fill the centuries between and around them — real, often influential gatherings, but never claiming the universal authority the twenty-one ecumenical councils carry.
Who Can Call One, and What Makes It Count

In the Church’s first thousand years, it was usually the Roman emperor who summoned an ecumenical council and paid for the bishops to travel — Constantine at Nicaea, Theodosius II at Ephesus, Marcian at Chalcedon.
The emperor convened; he did not teach.
What made a council’s decrees binding was never imperial power but reception by the Church, confirmed above all by the Bishop of Rome.
Later councils were called directly by popes — Trent by Paul III, the two Vatican councils by Pius IX and John XXIII.
Whoever calls the meeting, an ecumenical council’s teaching only becomes binding on the whole Church once the Pope confirms it.
A gathering of bishops that lacks that confirmation, however large, is not an ecumenical council in the Church’s own sense of the word.
What Councils Have Done
Councils give the Church her creeds.
The Nicene Creed, prayed every Sunday at Mass, was drafted at Nicaea in 325 and completed at Constantinople in 381.
Councils have also settled the Church’s most contested questions about who Christ is.
Ephesus in 431 defended Mary’s title Mother of God against Nestorius.
Chalcedon in 451 defined Christ as one Person in two natures, divine and human, ‘without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.’
Later councils turned to reform as much as doctrine.
Trent, meeting across nearly twenty years in the sixteenth century, answered the Protestant Reformation point by point while also reforming clerical training and worship.
The Second Vatican Council, four centuries later, renewed the Church’s engagement with the modern world without changing a single defined dogma.
When a Council Fails to Hold
Not every large gathering of bishops earns the name ecumenical council, even when it was convened with every intention of being one.
In 449, a synod met at Ephesus under Emperor Theodosius II and, through intimidation and manipulated proceedings, exonerated the heretic Eutyches and deposed several orthodox bishops.
Pope Leo the Great refused to accept its acts and branded it a Latrocinium — a ‘Robber Synod.’
Two years later, the Council of Chalcedon reversed its findings and became the fourth ecumenical council instead.
The episode is a useful reminder that a council’s authority was never simply a matter of bishops showing up in one place.
What makes an ecumenical council ecumenical is its recognition and confirmation by the Pope, together with the council's exercise of the Church's universal teaching authority in union with him.
One Voice, Across the Centuries
Twenty-one times now, across nearly two thousand years, the Church has gathered her bishops to speak with one voice on a question that mattered too much to leave unanswered.
The councils on this timeline are not a record of the Church debating herself into existence.
They are the record of a Church that has always trusted Christ’s promise that the Spirit would lead her into all truth — one difficult, contested, hard-won council at a time.
